note: A card where the model and the market disagree on five winners. I side with the model on its strongest reads and depart where its data is thin or it can't see the context. Topuria and Matthews: the model leans on regional records and a layoff, while market and pundits strongly favour them. Hooker: Ortega has been out 15 months, withdrew twice and moves up a weight, which the stats can't see. Last week following the model on method and round would have scored more, so I only change those where a fighter's own record argues for it.

picks.why: Stirling is the faster, cleaner striker, and Procházka gets hit a lot: he was stopped in R2 twice by Pereira and in R1 by Ulberg. Procházka is at his most dangerous in the opening minutes, wild and swinging, so Stirling counters through that round and finishes him in R2 once the exchanges open up. Three of Stirling's finishes came in R2.

The model's pick. Sterling is 37, said he was 'dying' on the cut, and has been stopped by explosive strikers. Nine of Vallejos's finishes came in R1. Sterling has to shoot early to win, and that is where Vallejos catches him coming in. Sterling's back-taking is the real risk, so the confidence stays modest.

An override of the model's Ortega pick, for what the stats can't see. Ortega has been out about 15 months, withdrew from two bookings this year with injuries, and is making his first walk at 155. Hooker is the bigger, busier lightweight on a full camp. Ortega's guillotine and R3 submissions are real, but Hooker's volume should win him the rounds, so a decision.

Horiguchi's speed and takedown defence keep the grinder at bay. Almabayev has never been finished early, and his only stoppage losses came in R3, so a decision, as the model has it. Eight of nine pundits agree.

Aliskerov wins by control: his last two were wrestling decisions with six and nine minutes on top. Cannonier, 42, has been stopped once since 2019 (Imavov, R4); every other loss went the distance. So Aliskerov over three rounds.

An override of the model, whose Luna number rests on a short UFC record. The market has Topuria at 71% and pundits 6 of 8. Topuria's Greco-Roman wrestling and BJJ against a 22-year-old who was submitted from his back by Mitchell. Both of Topuria's UFC wins were decisions, and Luna has been finished once, so Topuria on the cards.

The model's pick, against the market. Gaziev was knocked out in R1 and R2 in his last three, and all eight of Teixeira's finishes came in R1. Teixeira fades badly after R1, so if he wins it's early, and both chins make an early ending the likeliest outcome.

Close: the model still has Albazi after my small read toward Costa, and 5 of 7 pundits agree. Albazi knocked Costa out in their first fight, but he fights once a year and his takedowns have dried up. A tight decision is the likeliest result; Costa has been finished only once in R2 and once in R3.

An override: the model's Abdullayev number rests on a regional record that differs by source and one UFC fight. Matthews has 24 UFC fights and won his last clearly, while Abdullayev missed weight by a pound. Matthews grinds out rounds with his jiu-jitsu and top control, so a decision.

picks.bout: Nikolas Motta vs Dom Mar Fan
picks.why: Motta is 17 months out after a jaw broken badly enough to need titanium plates, and has little ground game. Fan's grappling controls a brawler over three rounds; neither finishes much late. A decision, as the model has it.

Nearly every fight Lorenz has had ended in R1, in either direction, and eight of Nurgozhay's finishes came in R1. The debutant's untested cardio doesn't come into it: an early ending, Nurgozhay's way.

Two short-notice debutants. The model has Yousaf: never stopped, all three losses on the cards, and his last three wins R1 knockouts. Mitchell is a boxer with five decision wins who has been stopped twice. I take Yousaf on the model's number, and a decision because neither has been finished by a fighter of this level.
